claim: Social deficit is a major feature of neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
source: Social deficit is a major feature of neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, but its neural mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about neuropsychiatric disorders.

claim: The neural mechanisms underlying social deficit in neuropsychiatric disorders remain unclear.
source: Social deficit is a major feature of neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, but its neural mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: IRSp53-mutant mice show social deficits.
source: Here, we examined neuronal discharge characteristics in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of IRSp53/Baiap2-mutant mice, which show social deficits, during social approach.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a decrease in the proportion of IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons encoding social information.
source: We found a decrease in the proportion of IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons encoding social information, but not that encoding non-social information.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The proportion of IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons encoding non-social information is not decreased.
source: We found a decrease in the proportion of IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons encoding social information, but not that encoding non-social information.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The firing activity of IRSp53-mutant neurons is less differential between social and non-social targets.
source: In addition, the firing activity of IRSp53-mutant neurons was less differential between social and non-social targets.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons display an increase in baseline neuronal firing.
source: IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons displayed an increase in baseline neuronal firing, but decreases in the variability and dynamic range of firing as well as burst firing during social and non-social target approaches compared to wild-type controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons display decreases in the variability of firing during social and non-social target approaches compared to wild-type controls.
source: IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons displayed an increase in baseline neuronal firing, but decreases in the variability and dynamic range of firing as well as burst firing during social and non-social target approaches compared to wild-type controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons display decreases in the dynamic range of firing during social and non-social target approaches compared to wild-type controls.

claim: IRSp53-mutant excitatory mPFC neurons display decreases in burst firing during social and non-social target approaches compared to wild-type controls.

claim: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist.
source: Treatment of memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist that rescues social deficit in IRSp53-mutant mice, alleviates the reduced burst firing of IRSp53-mutant pyramidal mPFC neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pharmacological properties of memantine.

claim: Memantine rescues social deficit in IRSp53-mutant mice.
source: Treatment of memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist that rescues social deficit in IRSp53-mutant mice, alleviates the reduced burst firing of IRSp53-mutant pyramidal mPFC neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Chung et al., 2015).

claim: Memantine treatment alleviates the reduced burst firing of IRSp53-mutant pyramidal mPFC neurons.
source: Treatment of memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist that rescues social deficit in IRSp53-mutant mice, alleviates the reduced burst firing of IRSp53-mutant pyramidal mPFC neurons.

claim: Suppressed neuronal activity dynamics may underlie impaired cortical encoding of social information in IRSp53-mutant mice.
source: These results suggest that suppressed neuronal activity dynamics and burst firing may underlie impaired cortical encoding of social information and social behaviors in IRSp53-mutant mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) plays critical roles in integrative and higher cognitive brain functions.
source: Among the various brain regions involved in social regulation, the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) plays critical roles in integrative and higher cognitive brain functions (Yan and Rein, 2022; Yizhar and Levy, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An imbalance of neuronal excitation/inhibition is associated with dysfunctions under a social context.
source: Examples include an imbalance of neuronal excitation/inhibition (Selimbeyoglu et al., 2017; Yizhar et al., 2011) (reviewed in Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019), impaired cortical social representation (Lee et al., 2021a; Lee et al., 2021b; Lee et al., 2016; Levy et al., 2019; Miura et al., 2020), and the disruption of local oscillations (Cao et al., 2018; Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Impaired cortical social representation is associated with dysfunctions under a social context.
source: Examples include an imbalance of neuronal excitation/inhibition (Selimbeyoglu et al., 2017; Yizhar et al., 2011) (reviewed in Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019), impaired cortical social representation (Lee et al., 2021a; Lee et al., 2021b; Lee et al., 2016; Levy et al., 2019; Miura et al., 2020), and the disruption of local oscillations (Cao et al., 2018; Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The disruption of local oscillations is associated with dysfunctions under a social context.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 is encoded by the BAIAP2 gene.
source: Insulin receptor substrate protein 53 kDa (IRSp53) encoded by the BAIAP2 gene is a postsynaptic scaffolding and adaptor protein at excitatory synapses that interacts with other key components of the postsynaptic density such as PSD-95 (Choi et al., 2005; Soltau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IRSp53 is a postsynaptic scaffolding and adaptor protein at excitatory synapses.
source: Insulin receptor substrate protein 53 kDa (IRSp53) encoded by the BAIAP2 gene is a postsynaptic scaffolding and adaptor protein at excitatory synapses that interacts with other key components of the postsynaptic density such as PSD-95 (Choi et al., 2005; Soltau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IRSp53 interacts with PSD-95.

claim: IRSp53 deficiency in mice leads to excitatory synaptic deficits.
source: IRSp53 deficiency in mice leads to excitatory synaptic deficits and various behavioral deficits, including hyperactivity, cognitive impairments, and social deficits (Bobsin and Kreienkamp, 2016; Chung et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2020b; Sawallisch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 deficiency in mice leads to hyperactivity.
source: IRSp53 deficiency in mice leads to excitatory synaptic deficits and various behavioral deficits, including hyperactivity, cognitive impairments, and social deficits (Bobsin and Kreienkamp, 2016; Chung et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2020b; Sawallisch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 deficiency in mice leads to cognitive impairments.
source: IRSp53 deficiency in mice leads to excitatory synaptic deficits and various behavioral deficits, including hyperactivity, cognitive impairments, and social deficits (Bobsin and Kreienkamp, 2016; Chung et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2020b; Sawallisch et al., 2009).

claim: IRSp53 knockout mice have fewer dendritic spines.
source: IRSp53 knockout (KO) mice have fewer dendritic spines and enhanced NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function; they show impaired social behavior that is rescued by pharmacological NMDAR suppression (Chung et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009).

claim: IRSp53 knockout mice have enhanced NMDA receptor function.
source: IRSp53 knockout (KO) mice have fewer dendritic spines and enhanced NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function; they show impaired social behavior that is rescued by pharmacological NMDAR suppression (Chung et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 knockout mice show impaired social behavior that is rescued by pharmacological NMDAR suppression.
source: IRSp53 knockout (KO) mice have fewer dendritic spines and enhanced NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function; they show impaired social behavior that is rescued by pharmacological NMDAR suppression (Chung et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009).

claim: mPFC neurons in IRSp53-KO mice show reduced neuronal firing under urethane-anesthesia.
source: Importantly, mPFC neurons in IRSp53-KO mice show reduced neuronal firing under urethane-anesthesia, which is acutely normalized by pharmacological NMDAR suppression (Chung et al., 2015).

source: However, it remained unknown whether and how the social behavioral deficits are associated with altered mPFC neural activity in waking-state animals engaged in social interaction.

claim: WT and IRSp53-KO mice showed a preference for neither chamber in the E-E session, as assessed by in-zone duration.

source: In the second S-O session, WT mice no longer displayed social preference, likely because of social habituation (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

claim: IRSp53-KO mice showed a decreased number of sniffing visits to the social conspecific mouse.

claim: The mean duration of each sniffing visit in IRSp53-KO mice was comparable to that of the WT mice.

claim: The impaired social preference in IRSp53-KO mice is less likely to be caused by genotypic differences in olfactory processing speeds.

claim: Total durations of both proximal and distal social interactions were not reduced in IRSp53-KO mice during the second S-O session.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There was an increase in the duration of distal object interaction in IRSp53-KO mice during the first S-O session.

claim: There was no increase in the duration of proximal object interaction in IRSp53-KO mice during the first S-O session.

claim: There was no genotype difference in object interaction duration in the second S-O session.

claim: The relative amounts of time spent for proximal versus distal interactions did not vary across genotypes during social sniffing.

claim: IRSp53-KO mice display social impairments in the linear social-interaction chamber.
source: These behavioral results collectively indicate that IRSp53-KO mice display social impairments in the linear social-interaction chamber, similar to the social impairments previously determined using the three-chamber test, direct/dyadic social-interaction test, and ultrasonic vocalization test (Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and citation to previous work.

claim: The firing rate of total neurons at rest was higher in the mPFC of IRSp53-KO mice compared with WT mice.
source: The firing rate of total neurons at rest was higher in the mPFC of IRSp53-KO mice compared with WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only the IRSp53-KO pExc neurons, but not IRSp53-KO pInh neurons, showed a significant increase in firing rate at rest.
source: However, only the IRSp53-KO pExc neurons, but not IRSp53-KO pInh neurons, showed a significant increase in firing rate (Figure 2D and E), suggesting that pExc neurons mainly contribute to the increase in the total firing rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: pExc neurons mainly contribute to the increase in the total firing rate in IRSp53-KO mice at rest.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The results from awake, behaving mice differ from those previously obtained from anesthetized IRSp53-KO mice.
source: These results differ from those previously obtained from anesthetized IRSp53-KO mice (Chung et al., 2015), which exhibited decreases in total and pExc firing.
evidence: This is a comparison between current data and previous work cited.

claim: Anesthetized IRSp53-KO mice exhibited decreases in total and pExc firing.
source: These results differ from those previously obtained from anesthetized IRSp53-KO mice (Chung et al., 2015), which exhibited decreases in total and pExc firing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is important to measure cortical neuronal activity in awake, behaving mice.
source: This highlights the importance of measuring cortical neuronal activity in awake, behaving mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the difference between awake and anesthetized recordings.

claim: A significantly lower proportion was classified as social neurons among IRSp53-KO pExc neurons compared to WT pExc neurons.

claim: The proportions of object and empty neurons were comparable between genotypes.

claim: Reduction in social/non-social neuronal proportion in mPFC is a phenomenon that is shared by several autism mouse models.
source: Reduction in social/non-social neuronal proportion in mPFC is a phenomenon that is shared by several autism mouse models, such as Shank2-KO (Lee et al., 2021a) and Cntnap2-KO mice (Levy et al., 2019), and therefore, may be causally related to the social impairment seen in IRSp53-KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and inference about causality.

claim: The reduction in social/non-social neuronal proportion in mPFC may be causally related to the social impairment seen in IRSp53-KO mice.
source: Reduction in social/non-social neuronal proportion in mPFC is a phenomenon that is shared by several autism mouse models, such as Shank2-KO (Lee et al., 2021a) and Cntnap2-KO mice (Levy et al., 2019), and therefore, may be causally related to the social impairment seen in IRSp53-KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data and comparison with other models.

claim: The firing responses of WT and IRSp53-KO mPFC pExc neurons to social, object, and sidedness were consistent across the first and second S-O sessions.

claim: Both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons showed significantly higher response magnitudes during proximal than distal interactions with social and object targets.

claim: Social neurons in the mPFC display 'trial-to-trial stochasticity'.

claim: Both WT and IRSp53-KO target neurons displayed trial consistencies that are higher than 50%.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The responses of social and object neurons to the targets do not occur by chance.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trial consistency data.

claim: The consistencies in firing rate responses to proximal target interactions were comparable between WT and IRSp53-KO mice.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The absolute difference in firing rate for S versus O in the first S-O session was significantly lower in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons than WT pExc neurons.

claim: IRSp53-KO pExc neurons could still discriminate between social and object targets significantly better compared to the left versus right side discrimination in the E-E session.
source: Nevertheless, IRSp53-KO pExc neurons could still discriminate between social and object targets significantly better compared to the left versus right side discrimination in the E-E session (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IRSp53-KO mice have the ability to recognize social and object stimuli, albeit in a reduced degree than WT mice.
source: This result suggests that IRSp53-KO mice have the ability to recognize social and object stimuli, albeit in a reduced degree than WT mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the discriminability data.

claim: The decoding performances of individual neurons and neuronal population were significantly lower in IRSp53-KO neurons for social versus object target discriminability in the first S-O session.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the second S-O session, the individual neurons' decoding performances were comparable between genotypes.
source: In the second S-O session, although the individual neurons' decoding performances were comparable between genotypes, population decoding performances were significantly poorer in IRSp53-KO than WT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In the second S-O session, population decoding performances were significantly poorer in IRSp53-KO than WT neurons.
source: In the second S-O session, although the individual neurons' decoding performances were comparable between genotypes, population decoding performances were significantly poorer in IRSp53-KO than WT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The discriminability between social and object targets was generally greater during proximal interaction compared to distal interaction.
source: Moreover, we examined whether the discriminability between social and object targets is affected by the proximity to the target. Although the discriminability was generally greater during proximal interaction compared to distal interaction, the discriminability in KO neurons was lower in both proximal and distal conditions compared to that in WT neurons in the first S-O session (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The discriminability in KO neurons was lower in both proximal and distal conditions compared to that in WT neurons in the first S-O session.
source: Moreover, we examined whether the discriminability between social and object targets is affected by the proximity to the target. Although the discriminability was generally greater during proximal interaction compared to distal interaction, the discriminability in KO neurons was lower in both proximal and distal conditions compared to that in WT neurons in the first S-O session (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The discriminability was no longer different between genotypes during the distal social condition in the second S-O session.
source: However, the discriminability was no longer different between genotypes during the distal social condition in the second S-O session (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The pExc mPFC neurons of IRSp53-KO mice showed significantly higher mean firing rates than those of WT mice during the initial 5-min rest period.
source: The pExc mPFC neurons of IRSp53-KO mice showed significantly higher mean firing rates than those of WT mice during the initial 5-min rest period (Figure 2D), but comparable mean firing rates during the 30 min linear chamber test period (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The pExc mPFC neurons of IRSp53-KO mice showed comparable mean firing rates to WT mice during the 30 min linear chamber test period.
source: The pExc mPFC neurons of IRSp53-KO mice showed significantly higher mean firing rates than those of WT mice during the initial 5-min rest period (Figure 2D), but comparable mean firing rates during the 30 min linear chamber test period (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The maximum instantaneous firing rate during the linear chamber test was significantly lower in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons than WT pExc neurons.
source: Further examinations of instantaneous firing rate revealed that the maximum instantaneous firing rate during the linear chamber test was significantly lower in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons than WT pExc neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There was a trend for higher minimum instantaneous firing rates in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons than WT pExc neurons.
source: In contrast, there was a trend for higher minimum instantaneous firing rates in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons than WT pExc neurons (p=0.0544; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The dynamic range of firing rate during the linear chamber test was significantly narrower for IRSp53-KO pExc neurons than WT pExc neurons.
source: Consequently, the dynamic range of firing rate (the difference between the maximum and minimum instantaneous firing rates) during the linear chamber test was significantly narrower for IRSp53-KO pExc neurons than WT pExc neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The firing-rate range significantly increases from the E-E session to the first and second S-O sessions in WT neurons.
source: While the firing-rate range significantly increases from the E-E session to the first and second S-O sessions in WT neurons, these changes in firing-rate range were not observed in KO neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Changes in firing-rate range from the E-E session to the first and second S-O sessions were not observed in KO neurons.
source: While the firing-rate range significantly increases from the E-E session to the first and second S-O sessions in WT neurons, these changes in firing-rate range were not observed in KO neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The firing-rate range is comparable between genotypes in the resting state.
source: Although the firing-rate range is comparable between genotypes in the resting state, it was significantly narrower in IRSp53-KO than WT mPFC neurons in both E-E (non-social) and S-O (social) conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The firing-rate range was significantly narrower in IRSp53-KO than WT mPFC neurons in both E-E (non-social) and S-O (social) conditions.
source: Although the firing-rate range is comparable between genotypes in the resting state, it was significantly narrower in IRSp53-KO than WT mPFC neurons in both E-E (non-social) and S-O (social) conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: The limited firing-rate range in IRSp53-KO neurons is most salient during, but not restricted to, the social condition.
source: These results suggest that the limited firing-rate range in IRSp53-KO neurons is most salient during, but not restricted to, the social condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: IRSp53-KO neurons had a significantly lower proportion of time-bins in the lowest firing rate (0–0.1) compared to WT neurons.
source: As expected, IRSp53-KO neurons had a significantly lower proportion of time-bins in the lowest firing rate (0–0.1) and instead higher proportions in mid-range firing rates (0.2–0.6) compared to the WT neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: IRSp53-KO neurons had higher proportions in mid-range firing rates (0.2–0.6) compared to the WT neurons.
source: As expected, IRSp53-KO neurons had a significantly lower proportion of time-bins in the lowest firing rate (0–0.1) and instead higher proportions in mid-range firing rates (0.2–0.6) compared to the WT neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The instantaneous firing rates of IRSp53-KO neurons were less variable, as indicated by a decrease in the sigma value.
source: We found that the instantaneous firing rates of IRSp53-KO neurons were indeed less variable, as indicated by a decrease in the sigma value (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: IRSp53-KO neurons were generally less variable in instantaneous firing activity regardless of their mean discharge rate.
source: In order to test if this decrease in variability in IRSp53-KO neurons is dependent upon the mean firing rate, the relationship between mean firing rates and sigma values was compared between genotypes (Figure 5F). As indicated by the significant decrease in the intercept—and comparable slope— of the linear regression, IRSp53-KO neurons were generally less variable in instantaneous firing activity regardless of their mean discharge rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The decrease in sigma value was observed consistently across the analyses using variable sizes of time window for calculating instantaneous firing rate, ranging from 0.5 to 5 s.
source: This decrease in sigma value was observed consistently across the analyses using variable sizes of time window for calculating instantaneous firing rate, ranging from 0.5 to 5 s (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The reduced variability was specific to the recordings from social conditions but not the rest period and non-social conditions.
source: The reduced variability was specific to the recordings from social conditions but not the rest period and non-social conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L.

claim: WT neurons showed increased variability in instantaneous firing rate during the first S-O session compared to the E-E session.
source: Similar to firing-rate range, WT neurons showed increased variability in instantaneous firing rate during the first S-O session compared to the E-E session, while IRSp53-KO neurons showed similar levels of variability across the three sessions (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: IRSp53-KO neurons showed similar levels of variability across the three sessions.
source: Similar to firing-rate range, WT neurons showed increased variability in instantaneous firing rate during the first S-O session compared to the E-E session, while IRSp53-KO neurons showed similar levels of variability across the three sessions (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: IRSp53-KO mice displayed a decreased maximum Δ firing rate only in the first S-O session of the linear-chamber test, but not in the E-E or second S-O session.
source: Compared to WT mice, IRSp53-KO mice displayed a decreased maximum Δ firing rate only in the first S-O session of the linear-chamber test, but not in the E-E or second S-O session (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: IRSp53-KO pExc neurons showed a general decrease in the normalized maximum Δ firing rate across all three sessions.
source: IRSp53-KO pExc neurons showed a general decrease in the normalized maximum Δ firing rate across all three sessions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The response magnitudes of both WT and IRSp53-KO pExc neurons were the highest during the first S-O session, in response to novel social and object targets.
source: It is notable that the response magnitudes of both WT and IRSp53-KO pExc neurons were the highest during the first S-O session, in response to novel social and object targets.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There was a pronounced reduction in the proportion of ISIs ≤10ms in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons during the linear chamber test.
source: Contrary to the comparable levels of average ISI histograms between WT and IRSp53-KO pExc neurons at rest, those during the linear chamber test varied across genotype. In particular, there was a pronounced reduction in the proportion of ISIs ≤10ms in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The ability to exhibit an abrupt increase in firing rate may be impaired in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons.
source: This result suggests that the ability to exhibit an abrupt increase in firing rate may be impaired in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ISI data.

claim: Burst firing increased significantly during the linear chamber-exploring state compared to the resting state in WT pExc neurons.
source: We found that burst firing increased significantly during the linear chamber-exploring state compared to the resting state in WT pExc neurons. Such change, however, was not observed in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The increase in burst firing during the linear chamber-exploring state compared to the resting state was not observed in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons.
source: We found that burst firing increased significantly during the linear chamber-exploring state compared to the resting state in WT pExc neurons. Such change, however, was not observed in IRSp53-KO pExc neurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Burst firing did not differ significantly between WT and IRSp53-KO pExc neurons during the rest period.
source: Burst firing did not differ significantly between WT and IRSp53-KO pExc neurons during the rest period, but was significantly lower in IRSp53-KO than WT pExc neurons during the linear chamber exploration (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Burst firing was significantly lower in IRSp53-KO than WT pExc neurons during the linear chamber exploration.
source: Burst firing did not differ significantly between WT and IRSp53-KO pExc neurons during the rest period, but was significantly lower in IRSp53-KO than WT pExc neurons during the linear chamber exploration (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Decreased burst firing in IRSp53-KO neurons was observed in both social and non-social conditions.
source: Similar to the firing-rate range, decreased burst firing in IRSp53-KO neurons was observed in both social and non-social conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: After burst elimination, the variability, firing-rate range, and response magnitude to social and object targets during the first S-O session remained to be reduced in IRSp53-KO neurons.
source: After burst elimination, the variability, firing-rate range, and response magnitude to social and object targets during the first S-O session remained to be reduced in IRSp53-KO neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: The abilities to discriminate between left and right sidedness and social and object targets were maintained in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons after burst elimination.
source: The abilities to discriminate between left and right sidedness and social and object targets were also maintained in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons, although the decoding performance of IRSp53-KO neurons still remained to be lower than that of WT neurons for target discrimination (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: The decoding performance of IRSp53-KO neurons still remained to be lower than that of WT neurons for target discrimination after burst elimination.
source: The abilities to discriminate between left and right sidedness and social and object targets were also maintained in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons, although the decoding performance of IRSp53-KO neurons still remained to be lower than that of WT neurons for target discrimination (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: Burst spikes increase the probability of post-neuronal spike more effectively than tonic spikes.
source: Although these results seem to suggest the unimportance of burst on social information encoding, it is well known that burst spikes increase the probability of post-neuronal spike more effectively than tonic spikes (Krahe and Gabbiani, 2004; Lisman, 1997), and that simple elimination of burst spikes, post-recording, do not eliminate the real-time effects of burst on neighboring neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Simple elimination of burst spikes, post-recording, do not eliminate the real-time effects of burst on neighboring neurons.
source: Although these results seem to suggest the unimportance of burst on social information encoding, it is well known that burst spikes increase the probability of post-neuronal spike more effectively than tonic spikes (Krahe and Gabbiani, 2004; Lisman, 1997), and that simple elimination of burst spikes, post-recording, do not eliminate the real-time effects of burst on neighboring neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of post-hoc analysis.

claim: The spike variability, firing-rate range, and response magnitude to social and object targets were still reduced in the KO neurons after tonic spike elimination.
source: The spike variability, firing-rate range, and response magnitude to social and object targets were still reduced in the KO neurons after tonic spike elimination (Figure 6—figure supplement 2I–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2I–L.

claim: The decoding performance between social and object targets was maintained in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons after tonic spike elimination, and still lower in the KO neurons.
source: In addition, the decoding performance between social and object targets was maintained in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons, and still lower in the KO neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2N.

claim: The left versus right side discriminability during the E-E session was maintained by the burst spikes in WT neurons but not in KO neurons.
source: Interestingly, the left versus right side discriminability during the E-E session was maintained by the burst spikes in WT neurons but not in KO neurons, suggesting that burst spikes may also play a role in side discriminability (Figure 6—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2M.

claim: Burst spikes may play a role in side discriminability.
source: Interestingly, the left versus right side discriminability during the E-E session was maintained by the burst spikes in WT neurons but not in KO neurons, suggesting that burst spikes may also play a role in side discriminability (Figure 6—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Tonic spikes may be sufficient for overcoming the weakness in left versus right side discriminability in IRSp53-KO neurons.
source: While the reduced burst in IRSp53-KO neurons may affect left versus right side discriminability, tonic spikes may be sufficient for overcoming this weakness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Tonic spikes may not be sufficient to overcome the weakened social versus object discriminability in KO neurons.
source: On the other hand, tonic spikes may not be sufficient to overcome the weakened social versus object discriminability in KO neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: WT and IRSp53-KO neurons did not display a genotype difference in baseline firing when neuronal firing was induced by current injection in layer 5 pyramidal neurons in the prelimbic mPFC.
source: When neuronal firing was induced by current injection in layer 5 pyramidal neurons in the prelimbic mPFC, WT and IRSp53-KO neurons did not display a genotype difference in baseline firing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There were no genotype differences in action potential-related parameters, including input resistance, AP threshold, AP amplitude, full width at half maximum, and afterhyperpolarization amplitude.
source: In addition, there were no genotype differences in action potential (AP)-related parameters, including input resistance, AP threshold, AP amplitude, full width at half maximum (FWHM), and afterhyperpolarization (AHP) amplitude (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Interspike interval analysis indicated a decreasing tendency of burst firing in IRSp53-KO neurons in slice electrophysiology.
source: Interspike interval (ISI) analysis indicated a decreasing tendency of burst firing (ISI <10ms) in IRSp53-KO neurons, as indicated by burst proportion (proportion of spikes in bursts) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and H), similar to the results from in vivo recording (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Upon memantine treatment, WT or IRSp53-KO neurons displayed largely unaltered current-firing curve and AP-related parameters, compared with untreated neurons.
source: Upon memantine treatment, WT or IRSp53-KO neurons displayed largely unaltered current-firing curve and AP-related parameters, compared with untreated neurons (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Memantine induced increases in FWHM in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons.
source: However, memantine induced increases in FWHM in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons and in AP amplitude in IRSp53-KO but not WT neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E), which may contribute to the increasing tendency of current-firing curve in memantine-treated WT and IRSp53-KO neurons (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Memantine induced increases in AP amplitude in IRSp53-KO but not WT neurons.
source: However, memantine induced increases in FWHM in both WT and IRSp53-KO neurons and in AP amplitude in IRSp53-KO but not WT neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E), which may contribute to the increasing tendency of current-firing curve in memantine-treated WT and IRSp53-KO neurons (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Memantine treatment induced opposite changes in burst proportion in WT and IRSp53-KO neurons.
source: Importantly, memantine treatment induced opposite changes in burst proportion in WT and IRSp53-KO neurons; memantine decreased burst proportion in WT neurons, whereas it increased burst proportion in IRSp53-KO neurons (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D–G.

claim: Memantine decreased burst proportion in WT neurons.
source: Importantly, memantine treatment induced opposite changes in burst proportion in WT and IRSp53-KO neurons; memantine decreased burst proportion in WT neurons, whereas it increased burst proportion in IRSp53-KO neurons (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D–G.

claim: Memantine increased burst proportion in IRSp53-KO neurons.
source: Importantly, memantine treatment induced opposite changes in burst proportion in WT and IRSp53-KO neurons; memantine decreased burst proportion in WT neurons, whereas it increased burst proportion in IRSp53-KO neurons (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D–G.

claim: Memantine treatment does not affect total firing in WT or IRSp53-KO neurons.
source: These results collectively suggest that memantine treatment does not affect total firing in WT or IRSp53-KO neurons whereas it induces opposite changes in burst firing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Memantine treatment seems to shift the balance more towards burst firing in IRSp53-KO neurons, increasing the reduced burst firing.
source: Memantine treatment seems to shift the balance more towards burst firing in IRSp53-KO neurons, increasing the reduced burst firing, which may be associated with the normalization of social deficit in IRSp53-KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The shift in balance towards burst firing in IRSp53-KO neurons by memantine may be associated with the normalization of social deficit in IRSp53-KO mice.
source: Memantine treatment seems to shift the balance more towards burst firing in IRSp53-KO neurons, increasing the reduced burst firing, which may be associated with the normalization of social deficit in IRSp53-KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and previous findings.

claim: Decreased firing rate variability, limited dynamic range, and decreased burst firing in IRSp53-KO putative excitatory mPFC neurons are accompanied by significant decrease in social-responsive neurons.
source: A key finding of the study is that decreased firing rate variability, limited dynamic range, and decreased burst firing in IRSp53-KO putative excitatory mPFC neurons are accompanied by significant decrease in social-responsive neurons and reduced decoding performance discriminating social and non-social cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings supported by experimental data.

claim: Decreased firing rate variability, limited dynamic range, and decreased burst firing in IRSp53-KO putative excitatory mPFC neurons are accompanied by reduced decoding performance discriminating social and non-social cues.
source: A key finding of the study is that decreased firing rate variability, limited dynamic range, and decreased burst firing in IRSp53-KO putative excitatory mPFC neurons are accompanied by significant decrease in social-responsive neurons and reduced decoding performance discriminating social and non-social cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings supported by experimental data.

claim: Reduced ratios of social/non-social encoding neurons may contribute to social deficits.
source: The most salient feature observed herein for IRSp53-KO mPFC neurons is a low proportion of social neurons, but not the other target neurons. This finding suggests that reduced ratios of social/non-social encoding neurons may contribute to social deficits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Similar disruptions in cortical representation of social contexts have been reported in previous studies on mouse models of ASD.
source: Similar disruptions in cortical representation of social contexts have been reported in previous studies on mouse models of ASD (Lee et al., 2021a; Lee et al., 2021b; Levy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Weakened response during social exploration is observed in mouse models with social deficits.
source: In addition, weakened response during social exploration is observed in mouse models with social deficits (Brumback et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A change in the intrinsic excitability is unlikely to cause the increased baseline firing in resting conditions in IRSp53-KO mPFC neurons.
source: It is unclear how this increase is caused. A change in the intrinsic excitability is unlikely because baseline firing was not changed in IRSp53-KO mPFC layer 5 neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The increased baseline firing in resting conditions might make the mutant neurons 'noisier' or have limited dynamic firing range, disrupting the reliable filtration and transduction of important signals.
source: Although further details remain to be determined, the increased baseline firing in resting conditions might make the mutant neurons 'noisier' or have limited dynamic firing range, disrupting the reliable filtration and transduction of important signals, such as, social and sensory cues, as reported previously for Cntnap2-mutant mice (Levy et al., 2019) and Ptchd1-mutant mice (Nakajima et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work on other mutant mice.

claim: Brain circuits are known to be more active during the awake state, compared to an anesthetized state.
source: Brain circuits are known to be more active during the awake state, compared to an anesthetized state (Albrecht and Davidowa, 1989; Shumkova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Urethane has diverse effects on neurotransmitter receptors and neuronal excitability.
source: In addition, urethane has diverse effects on neurotransmitter receptors (GABA, glycine, acetylcholine, NMDA, and AMPA receptors) and neuronal excitability (Accorsi-Mendonça et al., 2007; Hara and Harris, 2002; Sceniak and Maciver, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: IRSp53 is expressed primarily in the excitatory pyramidal neurons of the cortex.
source: Because IRSp53 is expressed primarily in the excitatory pyramidal (not inhibitory) neurons of the cortex (Burette et al., 2014), we hypothesized that the main effects of IRSp53 loss are seen in pExc neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The main effects of IRSp53 loss are seen in pExc neurons.
source: Because IRSp53 is expressed primarily in the excitatory pyramidal (not inhibitory) neurons of the cortex (Burette et al., 2014), we hypothesized that the main effects of IRSp53 loss are seen in pExc neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the expression pattern of IRSp53.

claim: IRSp53 deletion in mice alters excitatory synapse number and function in the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala.
source: IRSp53 deletion in mice alters excitatory synapse number and function in the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala (Bobsin and Kreienkamp, 2016; Chung et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2020b; Sawallisch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 deletion abnormally strengthens excitatory synaptic actin filaments.
source: IRSp53 deletion also abnormally strengthens excitatory synaptic actin filaments and NMDAR activity through impaired long-term depression of NMDARs (Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IRSp53 deletion abnormally strengthens NMDAR activity through impaired long-term depression of NMDARs.
source: IRSp53 deletion also abnormally strengthens excitatory synaptic actin filaments and NMDAR activity through impaired long-term depression of NMDARs (Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Actin modulatory proteins could have strong impacts on NMDAR function.
source: These results suggest that (1) actin modulatory proteins could have strong impacts on NMDAR function, supporting the reported link between dysregulated actin and mental disorders (Yan et al., 2016), (2) excessive NMDAR function could lead to social deficits, corroborating the NMDAR dysfunction hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2015a), (3) altered balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission could lead to social deficits, supporting the excitation/inhibition imbalance hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011), and (4) NMDAR modulators have a therapeutic potential for social dysfunction-related psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Excessive NMDAR function could lead to social deficits.
source: These results suggest that (1) actin modulatory proteins could have strong impacts on NMDAR function, supporting the reported link between dysregulated actin and mental disorders (Yan et al., 2016), (2) excessive NMDAR function could lead to social deficits, corroborating the NMDAR dysfunction hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2015a), (3) altered balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission could lead to social deficits, supporting the excitation/inhibition imbalance hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011), and (4) NMDAR modulators have a therapeutic potential for social dysfunction-related psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Altered balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission could lead to social deficits.
source: These results suggest that (1) actin modulatory proteins could have strong impacts on NMDAR function, supporting the reported link between dysregulated actin and mental disorders (Yan et al., 2016), (2) excessive NMDAR function could lead to social deficits, corroborating the NMDAR dysfunction hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2015a), (3) altered balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission could lead to social deficits, supporting the excitation/inhibition imbalance hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011), and (4) NMDAR modulators have a therapeutic potential for social dysfunction-related psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: NMDAR modulators have a therapeutic potential for social dysfunction-related psychiatric disorders.
source: These results suggest that (1) actin modulatory proteins could have strong impacts on NMDAR function, supporting the reported link between dysregulated actin and mental disorders (Yan et al., 2016), (2) excessive NMDAR function could lead to social deficits, corroborating the NMDAR dysfunction hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2015a), (3) altered balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission could lead to social deficits, supporting the excitation/inhibition imbalance hypothesis for ASD (Lee et al., 2017; Nelson and Valakh, 2015; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011), and (4) NMDAR modulators have a therapeutic potential for social dysfunction-related psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Decreased firing variability and burst firing may connect NMDAR dysfunction with prefrontal social encoding and behavioral social deficits in IRSp53-KO mice.
source: Our current results extend these findings by proposing that decreased firing variability and burst firing may connect NMDAR dysfunction with prefrontal social encoding and behavioral social deficits in IRSp53-KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Burst firing has been implicated in stronger presynaptic release, reliable synaptic transmission, synaptic plasticity, information processing, and neuropeptide release.
source: Burst firing has been implicated in stronger presynaptic release, reliable synaptic transmission, synaptic plasticity, information processing, and neuropeptide release (Cui et al., 2019; Krahe and Gabbiani, 2004; Lisman, 1997; Payeur et al., 2021).
